screens.title: Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the relational model and the S Q L basics you'll use every day. You will learn what tables, rows, columns, primary keys and foreign keys are, and why they matter for keeping data correct and linked. We will walk through how to define tables with CREATE TABLE, pick data types and constraints, insert rows, and run SELECT queries with WHERE filters. A short sqlite3 example shows these ideas in action, and a hands-on activity helps you practice creating tables, inserting records, and running queries. By the end you will be able to design a simple two-table schema that enforces referential integrity and run basic retrievals. A common misconception is that databases only store files; in contrast, relational databases model entities and relationships so we can ask precise questions like “which events did this user create” without copying user details into every row. Think of a table like a spreadsheet where each row is a single entity and each column is one attribute of that entity. As we proceed, notice how keys act like anchors for connections and how S Q L separates structure definition from data manipulation. Ready to build a small schema and run queries? Keep that spreadsheet image in mind and let’s dive into the details.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Relational Databases
Relational Databases and SQL Fundamentals
A compact guide to tables, keys, CREATE TABLE, INSERT, and SELECT so you can model and query related data safely.
In this lesson
Understand tables, keys, DDL, DML, and basic sqlite3 commands used to build and query schemas.
Why it matters
Relational design prevents inconsistent data and makes queries predictable, efficient, and maintainable.
Coming up
DDL example, DML examples, referential integrity, and a hands-on sqlite3 activity.
Explore Key Topics
Tables & Rows
Rows represent entities; columns represent attributes like username or email.
Keys & Relationships
Primary keys ensure uniqueness; foreign keys link tables and enforce integrity.
SQL: DDL & DML
Use CREATE TABLE to define structure and INSERT/SELECT to manipulate and retrieve data.
Visual: Table Cards
A Users table linked to Posts via a user_id foreign key.
Users
user_id, username, email, registration_date
Posts
post_id, user_id (FK), post_content, post_date
Quick example
CREATE a Users table with an integer primary key, then CREATE Posts with a foreign key that references Users. Insert rows and SELECT to retrieve linked data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map the practical skills you will practice. First, you will explain the relational model: why data is organized in tables of rows and columns, and how that model supports clear, queryable structures. Second, you will differentiate primary and foreign keys and describe their roles, so you can design schemas that prevent duplication and maintain referential integrity. Third, you will write basic Data Definition Language commands, specifically CREATE TABLE statements with appropriate column types and constraints. Fourth, you will compose basic Data Manipulation Language statements such as INSERT and SELECT with WHERE filters to add and retrieve rows. Each objective links a definition with a practical task: explaining the model, designing a key, writing DDL, and querying data. These skills matter because they let you create schemas that enforce rules and let you ask exact questions of your data. A common misconception is to duplicate data rather than reference it; practicing these objectives helps you prefer references and constraints so your data stays consistent. As you progress, look for the moment a foreign key prevents an invalid insert — that will confirm you understand referential integrity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Deep Practice
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on what good practice looks like as you apply these skills. First, when you design a table, aim for a single clear primary key that never repeats and cannot be NULL; this makes lookups efficient and unambiguous. Second, when you add a foreign key, ensure it references the exact primary key in the related table and that the database enforces this link to prevent orphaned rows. Third, practice writing CREATE TABLE statements that include sensible data types and defaults — defaults reduce missing values and make INSERT simpler. Fourth, craft SELECT queries with precise column lists and WHERE conditions so you return only the rows you need; this reduces data transfer and keeps results relevant. Each of these objectives pairs a definition with a practical check: design unique keys, test referential constraints, use defaults, and filter results. As you work through the sqlite3 activity, watch for constraint errors — they are not failures but confirmations that your schema is enforcing rules as intended.

screens.title: The Relational Model: Tables, Rows, and Columns
screens.narratorSegment: The relational model represents data as tables of rows and columns. A table, or relation, groups records that describe the same kind of entity — for example, a Users table for people or an Events table for scheduled gatherings. Each row is one record, often called a tuple, that captures all attributes for a single entity instance. Columns define the attributes or fields, such as username, email, or event_date, and they have types that limit the kind of values stored. This two-dimensional shape is powerful because it separates structure from content: the schema (columns and types) defines what values are valid, and the rows are the actual data. A helpful mental model is a spreadsheet where each sheet is a table: headers are column names and each row is an entity. A common misconception is to treat a table as a file full of varied documents; instead, each table should store one coherent entity type. For example, a Users table should not mix event details for two different logical entities. Keeping one entity per table simplifies queries and lets keys link related tables without copying repeated information. Concrete example: a Users table with columns user_id, username, email, and registration_date stores profile data for each user as one row per person. Misconception check: avoid storing emails for multiple users in a single freeform column — that breaks normalization. Key takeaway: model one entity per table, pick clear columns with types, and use rows to represent complete entity instances so your queries remain simple and reliable.

keyIdea.title: Table mental model
keyIdea.text: Think spreadsheet: each table groups one entity type, each row is one instance, and columns are typed attributes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Tables, Rows & Columns
Definition
A table stores many rows; each row is a single entity instance; columns define typed attributes for every row.
Analogy — Spreadsheet
Headers are column names, each row is a record. This helps you visualize queries as filters over rows.
Common mistake
Mixing unrelated entities in one table makes queries and constraints fragile. Keep one entity type per table.
Example
Users table
Columns: user_id (INTEGER), username (VARCHAR), email (VARCHAR), registration_date (DATE). Each row is one user.
Diagram: Annotated table
Row example
user_id: 1, username: alice_smith, email: alice@example.com, registration_date: 2023-01-15
Why types matter
Types like INTEGER and DATE limit invalid values and support correct comparisons in WHERE clauses.
Key Takeaway

Keep tables focused on one entity type; define columns with types so rows are consistent, searchable, and reliable.

screens.title: Primary Keys: Uniqueness and Non-null Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can be a single column or a combination of columns. The critical properties are uniqueness — no two rows share the same primary key value — and non-nullability — primary key columns cannot be empty. These properties let the database quickly locate a single record and enforce identity. In practice, numeric surrogate keys such as an INTEGER user_id are common because they are compact and efficient for indexing. Alternatively you might use a natural key like an email or username when it is guaranteed to be unique. A misconception is that any unique-looking column is automatically a good primary key; you should choose keys that remain stable over time and do not change frequently. For example, usernames might be changed by users, which makes them less ideal as primary keys than a generated numeric id. Concrete example: defining user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in CREATE TABLE gives you a simple, reliable identifier you can reference from other tables. If an insert attempts to add a duplicate primary key, the database rejects it, protecting data integrity. Key takeaway: pick a stable, unique, non-null column or set of columns as the primary key so rows are consistently addressable and relationships can be built on that identity.

keyIdea.title: Primary key rules
keyIdea.text: Primary keys must be unique and not NULL; prefer stable identifiers that don't change over time for reliable references.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Primary Keys
What is a primary key?
A primary key uniquely and permanently identifies rows so databases can enforce uniqueness and index efficiently.
Example definition
CREATE TABLE Users (
  user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
Misconception
Choosing a mutable field like username as the primary key can cause maintenance headaches when it must change. Prefer stable ids.
Key Takeaway

Primary keys are the stable identity anchor for rows; design them to be unique, non-null, and stable.

Concrete example
If Users.user_id is PRIMARY KEY, Posts can reference it as Posts.user_id. An attempted duplicate user_id insert will fail, protecting uniqueness.
Quick check
  • Is the key unique across all rows?
  • Can the key be NULL? It must not.
  • Will the key change frequently? If yes, choose another column.
Common mistake
Using readable fields that users edit as primary keys leads to cascade problems when you must update related rows.

screens.title: Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
screens.narratorSegment: Foreign keys create links between tables by storing a value in one table that refers to a primary key in another. This sets up referential integrity: the database prevents rows that reference missing parent rows. Imagine a Posts table with a user_id column that stores the author’s primary key from Users. If a post references user_id 42 but no user 42 exists, the foreign key constraint blocks that insert. This prevents orphaned records and ensures queries joining the tables return meaningful results. There are design considerations: foreign keys can be simple single-column references or composite across multiple columns. When designing relations, decide how to handle deletes and updates in the parent table — cascade, restrict, or set null — and choose the action that matches application needs. A common misconception is that foreign keys are optional decorations; in fact, they enforce the rule that a child row must have a valid parent, which is essential for data correctness. Concrete example: in CREATE TABLE Posts, declaring FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES Users(user_id) ensures every post points to an existing user. When you run an INSERT with a non-existent user_id, sqlite3 will raise an error if foreign keys are enforced, showing you the constraint in action. Key takeaway: use foreign keys to model real relationships and let the database enforce their validity so your data stays consistent and queries remain reliable.

keyIdea.title: Referential integrity
keyIdea.text: Foreign keys connect tables; constraints prevent child rows from referencing non-existent parent rows, protecting data consistency.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Foreign Keys
How it works
A foreign key column stores the primary key value from another table. The database ensures that the referenced parent row exists.
Example definition
CREATE TABLE Posts (
  post_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  post_content TEXT NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES Users(user_id)
);
Key Takeaway

Foreign keys are the mechanism that enforce relationships; use them to avoid orphan records and to allow safe joins.

Practical notes
  • Decide delete/update behavior: CASCADE, RESTRICT, or SET NULL.
  • Composite foreign keys reference composite primary keys when needed.
  • Enabling foreign key enforcement in sqlite3 is required for checks to run.
Common mistake
Not enabling foreign key enforcement in your client can make constraints appear ineffective; the schema definition only works when the engine enforces it.

screens.title: DDL: CREATE TABLE with Users and Posts
screens.narratorSegment: Data Definition Language commands define schema. CREATE TABLE is the primary DDL command you will use to specify table names, columns, data types, default values, and constraints like PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE. In practice, you write CREATE TABLE for each entity and explicitly state foreign keys to model relationships. Consider this concrete sqlite3 example: we create a Users table with user_id as INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and username and email as NOT NULL UNIQUE columns, plus registration_date with a DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE. Then we create Posts with a post_id primary key, a user_id column declared NOT NULL, and a FOREIGN KEY constraint referencing Users(user_id). This tells the database the allowed structure and enforces uniqueness and referential integrity. When you run CREATE TABLE, the database reserves the structure; no data is added yet. A common error is misspelling a column name referenced by a foreign key; the database will refuse to create the foreign key or will fail at insert time depending on the engine. Concrete example statements are displayed in the code panel here. After creating these tables, you can try inserting rows and watch how constraints accept or reject changes. Key takeaway: DDL creates the rules that protect your data before you ever insert a row.

keyIdea.title: DDL purpose
keyIdea.text: Use CREATE TABLE to declare columns, types, defaults and constraints so the database enforces structure and integrity.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › CREATE TABLE
DDL code: Users and Posts
-- DDL: Creating the Users table
CREATE TABLE Users (
  user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  registration_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- DDL: Creating the Posts table, linking to Users
CREATE TABLE Posts (
  post_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  post_content TEXT NOT NULL,
  post_date DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES Users(user_id)
);
Explanation
  • Specify types: INTEGER, VARCHAR, TEXT, DATE, DATETIME.
  • Use NOT NULL and UNIQUE to enforce value rules at the schema level.
  • Foreign key clauses link to the referenced primary key to enforce relationships.
Key Takeaway

CREATE TABLE defines the contract for your data. Write it carefully; it prevents many errors later.

screens.title: Data Types and Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Data types define what kind of values a column accepts and how the database stores and compares them. Common types shown in our examples include INTEGER for whole numbers, VARCHAR(n) for variable-length strings with a maximum length, TEXT for long strings, DATE for dates, and DATETIME for date-time values. Constraints like NOT NULL prevent empty values, UNIQUE prevents duplicates, PRIMARY KEY ensures uniqueness plus non-null, and DEFAULT provides a fallback when a value is omitted. Choosing appropriate types reduces invalid data and makes comparisons in WHERE clauses behave as expected: numeric comparisons on INTEGER, date comparisons on DATE, and string comparisons on VARCHAR or TEXT. A common mistake is using TEXT for everything to avoid thinking about types; while flexible, that can lead to subtle bugs when comparing dates or numbers. Concrete example: setting registration_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE means inserting users without an explicit date will automatically record the creation date, which reduces missing data. Another practical note: VARCHAR(n) sets an upper bound for storage and can express intention about expected lengths. Key takeaway: pick types that match the real-world property of the column and use constraints to codify business rules in the schema so invalid data is rejected early.

keyIdea.title: Types & rules
keyIdea.text: Choose column types that reflect real-world data and use constraints like NOT NULL, UNIQUE and DEFAULT to encode business rules in the schema.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Data Types & Constraints
Common data types
  • INTEGER — whole numbers, ideal for ids and counts
  • VARCHAR(n) — variable-length string with max characters
  • TEXT — longer strings
  • DATE / DATETIME — dates and timestamps for comparisons
Common constraints
  • NOT NULL — requires a value
  • UNIQUE — no duplicates allowed
  • PRIMARY KEY — unique + not null
  • DEFAULT — fills missing values automatically
Example: registration_date
Using DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE records when a user registered without requiring inserts to supply that field, reducing missing data and supporting date-based queries.
Key Takeaway

Match types to real-world values and use constraints to enforce rules; this reduces bugs and simplifies queries.

screens.title: DML: INSERTing Rows and Defaults in Action
screens.narratorSegment: Data Manipulation Language commands change table contents. INSERT adds rows, and the schema determines whether those inserts succeed. When you INSERT, columns declared NOT NULL must be supplied, UNIQUE constraints must not be violated, and foreign key constraints must reference existing parent rows. Defaults simplify INSERTs: if you omit a column with a DEFAULT, the database provides the default value. For example, inserting a user without registration_date will use CURRENT_DATE and succeed. Concrete examples: we insert three users with explicit ids and one where registration_date is omitted. If you attempt to insert a post with a user_id that does not exist in Users, the foreign key constraint will fail and the database will reject the insert. A common mistake is assuming the database will silently adjust values; instead, constraint violations must be fixed by the client. When you run multiple inserts, consider transactions so either all succeed or none do. Example INSERT statements are shown in the code panel. Key takeaway: INSERT obeys the rules defined by CREATE TABLE; read constraint errors as guidance about needed fixes rather than fatal surprises.

keyIdea.title: INSERT rules
keyIdea.text: INSERT must satisfy NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and foreign key constraints; DEFAULTs can reduce required fields during insert.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › INSERT
DML: INSERT examples
-- DML: Inserting data into the Users table
INSERT INTO Users (user_id, username, email, registration_date)
VALUES (1, 'alice_smith', 'alice@example.com', '2023-01-15');

INSERT INTO Users (user_id, username, email)
VALUES (2, 'bob_jones', 'bob@example.com'); -- registration_date uses DEFAULT

INSERT INTO Users (user_id, username, email)
VALUES (3, 'charlie_brown', 'charlie@example.com');

-- Attempting to insert a Post with a non-existent user_id will fail if FK enforced
INSERT INTO Posts (post_id, user_id, post_content)
VALUES (201, 999, 'Hello world'); -- may raise FK constraint error
Explanation & tips
  • Defaults fill missing values so fewer columns must be provided on INSERT.
  • Constraint errors tell you which rule was violated — fix the data or schema accordingly.
  • Wrap related INSERTs in a transaction to avoid partial state when multiple rows must be added together.
Key Takeaway

When inserting, follow the schema rules; defaults reduce boilerplate, and errors point you to needed schema or data fixes.

screens.title: SELECT Basics: Retrieving All Columns and Specific Columns
screens.narratorSegment: SELECT is the primary query used to read data. The simplest form SELECT * FROM table returns all columns for every row, which is useful for quick inspection but often returns more data than necessary. Better practice is to list specific columns you need, for example SELECT username, email FROM Users, which reduces data transferred and makes results easier to process. Use WHERE to filter rows — that will be covered next. A common misconception is to always use SELECT * because it’s convenient; in production, explicit columns are safer because schema changes won't silently break your caller code and you avoid returning unnecessary sensitive fields. Concrete example: SELECT * FROM Users; returns every column and row, whereas SELECT username, registration_date FROM Users WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'; only returns two columns and a filtered set of rows. Also remember S Q L keywords like SELECT and FROM are case-insensitive, while table and column name sensitivity depends on the database. Key takeaway: be deliberate with your SELECT column list to improve clarity, performance, and stability of queries. narration.text: SELECT is the primary query used to read data. The simplest form SELECT * FROM table returns all columns for every row, which is useful for quick inspection but often returns more data than necessary. Better practice is to list specific columns you need, for example SELECT username, email FROM Users, which reduces data transferred and makes results easier to process. Use WHERE to filter rows — that will be covered next. A common misconception is to always use SELECT * because it’s convenient; in production, explicit columns are safer because schema changes won't silently break your caller code and you avoid returning unnecessary sensitive fields. Concrete example: SELECT * FROM Users; returns every column and row, whereas SELECT username, registration_date FROM Users WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'; only returns two columns and a filtered set of rows. Also remember S Q L keywords like SELECT and FROM are case-insensitive, while table and column name sensitivity depends on the database. Key takeaway: be deliberate with your SELECT column list to improve clarity, performance, and stability of queries. keyIdea.text: Prefer explicit column lists over SELECT * to reduce unnecessary data and improve query robustness.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SELECT
Examples
-- Retrieve all columns and rows
SELECT * FROM Users;

-- Retrieve specific columns
SELECT username, email FROM Users;

-- Retrieve with a condition (covered next)
SELECT username, registration_date FROM Users
WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01';
Why choose columns explicitly?
  • Minimizes the amount of data returned.
  • Protects callers from schema changes that add or reorder columns.
  • Prevents accidental exposure of sensitive fields like emails if not needed.
Key Takeaway

Select only the columns you need. Explicit queries are clearer and more robust than SELECT *.

screens.title: Filtering Rows: WHERE Clause and Operators
screens.narratorSegment: The WHERE clause limits which rows a SELECT returns by applying conditions. These conditions use comparison operators such as equals, not equals, greater than, less than, and logical operators like AND, OR, and NOT to combine tests. For example, to find users who registered after January 1st, use WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'. To find users from a certain country who registered after a date, combine conditions with AND. LIKE supports simple pattern matching; for instance, WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%' finds names starting with J. A common misconception is that WHERE filters columns rather than rows; WHERE always evaluates per row and only rows satisfying the condition are returned. Another mistake is assuming comparisons work the same across types — comparing strings and dates differs from numeric comparisons, so choose types thoughtfully. Concrete examples: SELECT username, email FROM Users WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01' AND country = 'USA'; and SELECT first_name, last_name FROM Participants WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%'; Key takeaway: use WHERE with appropriate operators and types to retrieve precisely the rows you need, and validate your predicates against the column types to avoid unexpected results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › WHERE Clause
Examples
-- Users registered after a date
SELECT username, email FROM Users
WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01';

-- Events created by a specific participant
SELECT event_name, event_date FROM Events
WHERE creator_id = 1;

-- Names starting with 'J'
SELECT first_name, last_name FROM Participants
WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%';
Tip & common pitfalls

  • Be precise with AND vs OR to avoid returning too many or too few rows.
  • Test predicates with sample data to ensure expected results.
Key Takeaway

Use WHERE with correct operators and types to precisely filter rows; validate predicates on sample data to avoid surprises.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: sqlite3 Terminal Demo (Scripted Walkthrough)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough mirrors the activity instructions and shows what you'll type in sqlite3. Begin by launching sqlite3 events. db to create or open a database file. Then run the CREATE TABLE statements for Participants and Events. Notice the FOREIGN KEY clause in Events linking creator_id to Participants. participant_id. Insert several participant rows, then insert events that reference existing participant ids. If you try to insert an event with a non-existent creator_id, sqlite3 will raise a foreign key error when enforcement is enabled, demonstrating referential integrity. After inserts, run SELECT * FROM Participants; to inspect participants, SELECT event_name, event_date FROM Events WHERE creator_id = 1; to see a participant’s events, and SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM Participants WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%'; to filter by name. A practical tip is to enable foreign key enforcement in sqlite3 with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; so constraints are checked. Wrap multi-step inserts in a transaction to avoid partial state. Misconception check: seeing no error does not guarantee integrity unless foreign keys are enforced — confirm enforcement in your environment. Key takeaway: following these steps you will experience how schema rules accept valid data and block invalid data, reinforcing the role of DDL and constraints.

keyIdea.title: Terminal practice
keyIdea.text: Use sqlite3 to create tables, insert rows, enable foreign keys, and run SELECT queries to observe constraints and results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › sqlite3 Terminal Demo
Terminal: commands you will run
$ sqlite3 events.db
sqlite> PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
sqlite> -- Create tables
sqlite> CREATE TABLE Participants (
  participant_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  registration_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

sqlite> CREATE TABLE Events (
  event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  event_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  event_date DATETIME NOT NULL,
  location VARCHAR(100),
  creator_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (creator_id) REFERENCES Participants(participant_id)
);
Insert & query
sqlite> INSERT INTO Participants (participant_id, first_name, last_name, email) VALUES (1, 'Sarah', 'Connor', 'sarah.connor@example.com');
sqlite> INSERT INTO Events (event_id, event_name, event_date, location, creator_id) VALUES (101, 'Tech Meetup', '2023-11-15 18:00:00', 'Online', 1);
sqlite> SELECT * FROM Participants;
sqlite> SELECT event_name, event_date FROM Events WHERE creator_id = 1;
What you will observe
  • CREATE TABLE sets the schema; no data is added yet.
  • PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON ensures FK constraints are checked on INSERT.
  • An INSERT that violates a foreign key will be rejected with an error.
Key Takeaway

Running these commands in sqlite3 lets you experience schema enforcement: constraints protect data and queries return predictable results.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When working with relational schemas, several common errors recur. The most frequent are foreign key constraint failures, duplicate key violations, type mismatches, and forgetting to enable enforcement in your client. A foreign key error typically happens when you try to insert a child row referencing a parent id that doesn't exist; the fix is to insert the parent first or correct the referenced value. Duplicate key violations occur when you insert a row using a primary key already present; resolve this by using a new unique id or letting the database auto-generate the key if supported. Type mismatches appear when, for example, you compare strings to dates or insert a non-numeric value into an INTEGER column; ensure your client formats values according to the column types. Another subtle problem in sqlite3 is not turning on PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; without it, your schema's foreign key clauses exist but are not enforced during inserts. A troubleshooting workflow: read the error message carefully, identify the violated constraint, check the parent table for the referenced value, and re-run corrected statements. Concrete example: if inserting an event fails with a foreign key error for creator_id = 5, query Participants to see whether participant_id 5 exists, and if not, insert it first. Key takeaway: constraint errors are informative — use them as diagnostic signals to correct schema order or input values rather than seeing them as unexplained failures.

keyIdea.text: Use error messages to find violated constraints, verify parent rows exist, and confirm types and PRAGMA settings like foreign key enforcement.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Troubleshooting
Common errors
  • Foreign key constraint failed — referenced parent missing.
  • Unique constraint failed — duplicate primary or unique value.
  • Type mismatch — comparing or inserting incompatible types.
  • PRAGMA not enabled — constraints defined but not enforced.
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Read the exact error message from sqlite3 or your client.
  2. Query the parent table to check for the referenced key.
  3. Correct input values or insert parent rows first.
  4. Confirm PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON when using sqlite3.
Pro tip

Wrap related inserts in a transaction so either all rows are added or none are, avoiding partial states that trigger constraint chains.

Key Takeaway

Treat constraint errors as helpful diagnostics: fix the referenced data or schema order and re-run statements to restore integrity.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three concept cards summarize the foundations you will rely on. First, the Relational Model: data is organized into tables of rows and columns, modeling entities in a predictable two-dimensional structure. Second, Table and Row: a table groups entries of the same entity type, and each row is a single record representing an instance of that entity. Third, Column and Data Type: columns are named attributes with types like INTEGER, VARCHAR, DATE, or TEXT that limit acceptable values and guide how comparisons behave. Keep these ideas in mind as you design schemas so that structure and data types match real-world attributes and queries behave as you expect. A quick mental check is to ask whether each table stores one entity type and whether each column has a clear type and purpose.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: These three cards highlight keys and S Q L categories that structure how you build and operate on relational data. First, Primary Key: a unique, non-null column or columns that identify each row and support indexing and lookups. Second, Foreign Key: a column that references a primary key in another table to create relationships and enforce referential integrity. Third, S Q L categories — DDL and DML: DDL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE) defines schema and constraints; DML (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE) manipulates the data within those schemas. Remembering these distinctions helps you separate the act of defining structure from the act of changing data. A quick check: when you change a table's columns, you run DDL; when you add rows or query them, you use DML. Key takeaway: keys enforce identity and relationships, and S Q L provides distinct command families to define structure and to operate on rows.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the relational model and the S Q L basics you'll use every day. You will learn what tables, rows, columns, primary keys and foreign keys are, and why they matter for keeping data correct and linked. We will walk through how to define tables with CREATE TABLE, pick data types and constraints, insert rows, and run SELECT queries with WHERE filters. A short sqlite3 example shows these ideas in action, and a hands-on activity helps you practice creating tables, inserting records, and running queries. By the end you will be able to design a simple two-table schema that enforces referential integrity and run basic retrievals. A common misconception is that databases only store files; in contrast, relational databases model entities and relationships so we can ask precise questions like “which events did this user create” without copying user details into every row. Think of a table like a spreadsheet where each row is a single entity and each column is one attribute of that entity. As we proceed, notice how keys act like anchors for connections and how S Q L separates structure definition from data manipulation. Ready to build a small schema and run queries? Keep that spreadsheet image in mind and let’s dive into the details.

These learning objectives map the practical skills you will practice. First, you will explain the relational model: why data is organized in tables of rows and columns, and how that model supports clear, queryable structures. Second, you will differentiate primary and foreign keys and describe their roles, so you can design schemas that prevent duplication and maintain referential integrity. Third, you will write basic Data Definition Language commands, specifically CREATE TABLE statements with appropriate column types and constraints. Fourth, you will compose basic Data Manipulation Language statements such as INSERT and SELECT with WHERE filters to add and retrieve rows. Each objective links a definition with a practical task: explaining the model, designing a key, writing DDL, and querying data. These skills matter because they let you create schemas that enforce rules and let you ask exact questions of your data. A common misconception is to duplicate data rather than reference it; practicing these objectives helps you prefer references and constraints so your data stays consistent. As you progress, look for the moment a foreign key prevents an invalid insert — that will confirm you understand referential integrity.

This second objectives slide focuses on what good practice looks like as you apply these skills. First, when you design a table, aim for a single clear primary key that never repeats and cannot be NULL; this makes lookups efficient and unambiguous. Second, when you add a foreign key, ensure it references the exact primary key in the related table and that the database enforces this link to prevent orphaned rows. Third, practice writing CREATE TABLE statements that include sensible data types and defaults — defaults reduce missing values and make INSERT simpler. Fourth, craft SELECT queries with precise column lists and WHERE conditions so you return only the rows you need; this reduces data transfer and keeps results relevant. Each of these objectives pairs a definition with a practical check: design unique keys, test referential constraints, use defaults, and filter results. As you work through the sqlite3 activity, watch for constraint errors — they are not failures but confirmations that your schema is enforcing rules as intended.

The relational model represents data as tables of rows and columns. A table, or relation, groups records that describe the same kind of entity — for example, a Users table for people or an Events table for scheduled gatherings. Each row is one record, often called a tuple, that captures all attributes for a single entity instance. Columns define the attributes or fields, such as username, email, or event_date, and they have types that limit the kind of values stored. This two-dimensional shape is powerful because it separates structure from content: the schema (columns and types) defines what values are valid, and the rows are the actual data. A helpful mental model is a spreadsheet where each sheet is a table: headers are column names and each row is an entity. A common misconception is to treat a table as a file full of varied documents; instead, each table should store one coherent entity type. For example, a Users table should not mix event details for two different logical entities. Keeping one entity per table simplifies queries and lets keys link related tables without copying repeated information. Concrete example: a Users table with columns user_id, username, email, and registration_date stores profile data for each user as one row per person. Misconception check: avoid storing emails for multiple users in a single freeform column — that breaks normalization. Key takeaway: model one entity per table, pick clear columns with types, and use rows to represent complete entity instances so your queries remain simple and reliable.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can be a single column or a combination of columns. The critical properties are uniqueness — no two rows share the same primary key value — and non-nullability — primary key columns cannot be empty. These properties let the database quickly locate a single record and enforce identity. In practice, numeric surrogate keys such as an INTEGER user_id are common because they are compact and efficient for indexing. Alternatively you might use a natural key like an email or username when it is guaranteed to be unique. A misconception is that any unique-looking column is automatically a good primary key; you should choose keys that remain stable over time and do not change frequently. For example, usernames might be changed by users, which makes them less ideal as primary keys than a generated numeric id. Concrete example: defining user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in CREATE TABLE gives you a simple, reliable identifier you can reference from other tables. If an insert attempts to add a duplicate primary key, the database rejects it, protecting data integrity. Key takeaway: pick a stable, unique, non-null column or set of columns as the primary key so rows are consistently addressable and relationships can be built on that identity.

Foreign keys create links between tables by storing a value in one table that refers to a primary key in another. This sets up referential integrity: the database prevents rows that reference missing parent rows. Imagine a Posts table with a user_id column that stores the author’s primary key from Users. If a post references user_id 42 but no user 42 exists, the foreign key constraint blocks that insert. This prevents orphaned records and ensures queries joining the tables return meaningful results. There are design considerations: foreign keys can be simple single-column references or composite across multiple columns. When designing relations, decide how to handle deletes and updates in the parent table — cascade, restrict, or set null — and choose the action that matches application needs. A common misconception is that foreign keys are optional decorations; in fact, they enforce the rule that a child row must have a valid parent, which is essential for data correctness. Concrete example: in CREATE TABLE Posts, declaring FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES Users(user_id) ensures every post points to an existing user. When you run an INSERT with a non-existent user_id, sqlite3 will raise an error if foreign keys are enforced, showing you the constraint in action. Key takeaway: use foreign keys to model real relationships and let the database enforce their validity so your data stays consistent and queries remain reliable.

Data Definition Language commands define schema. CREATE TABLE is the primary DDL command you will use to specify table names, columns, data types, default values, and constraints like PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE. In practice, you write CREATE TABLE for each entity and explicitly state foreign keys to model relationships. Consider this concrete sqlite3 example: we create a Users table with user_id as INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and username and email as NOT NULL UNIQUE columns, plus registration_date with a DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE. Then we create Posts with a post_id primary key, a user_id column declared NOT NULL, and a FOREIGN KEY constraint referencing Users(user_id). This tells the database the allowed structure and enforces uniqueness and referential integrity. When you run CREATE TABLE, the database reserves the structure; no data is added yet. A common error is misspelling a column name referenced by a foreign key; the database will refuse to create the foreign key or will fail at insert time depending on the engine. Concrete example statements are displayed in the code panel here. After creating these tables, you can try inserting rows and watch how constraints accept or reject changes. Key takeaway: DDL creates the rules that protect your data before you ever insert a row.

Data types define what kind of values a column accepts and how the database stores and compares them. Common types shown in our examples include INTEGER for whole numbers, VARCHAR(n) for variable-length strings with a maximum length, TEXT for long strings, DATE for dates, and DATETIME for date-time values. Constraints like NOT NULL prevent empty values, UNIQUE prevents duplicates, PRIMARY KEY ensures uniqueness plus non-null, and DEFAULT provides a fallback when a value is omitted. Choosing appropriate types reduces invalid data and makes comparisons in WHERE clauses behave as expected: numeric comparisons on INTEGER, date comparisons on DATE, and string comparisons on VARCHAR or TEXT. A common mistake is using TEXT for everything to avoid thinking about types; while flexible, that can lead to subtle bugs when comparing dates or numbers. Concrete example: setting registration_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE means inserting users without an explicit date will automatically record the creation date, which reduces missing data. Another practical note: VARCHAR(n) sets an upper bound for storage and can express intention about expected lengths. Key takeaway: pick types that match the real-world property of the column and use constraints to codify business rules in the schema so invalid data is rejected early.

Data Manipulation Language commands change table contents. INSERT adds rows, and the schema determines whether those inserts succeed. When you INSERT, columns declared NOT NULL must be supplied, UNIQUE constraints must not be violated, and foreign key constraints must reference existing parent rows. Defaults simplify INSERTs: if you omit a column with a DEFAULT, the database provides the default value. For example, inserting a user without registration_date will use CURRENT_DATE and succeed. Concrete examples: we insert three users with explicit ids and one where registration_date is omitted. If you attempt to insert a post with a user_id that does not exist in Users, the foreign key constraint will fail and the database will reject the insert. A common mistake is assuming the database will silently adjust values; instead, constraint violations must be fixed by the client. When you run multiple inserts, consider transactions so either all succeed or none do. Example INSERT statements are shown in the code panel. Key takeaway: INSERT obeys the rules defined by CREATE TABLE; read constraint errors as guidance about needed fixes rather than fatal surprises.

SELECT is the primary query used to read data. The simplest form SELECT * FROM table returns all columns for every row, which is useful for quick inspection but often returns more data than necessary. Better practice is to list specific columns you need, for example SELECT username, email FROM Users, which reduces data transferred and makes results easier to process. Use WHERE to filter rows — that will be covered next. Concrete example: SELECT * FROM Users; returns every column and row, whereas SELECT username, registration_date FROM Users WHERE registration_date > '2023-01-01'; only returns two columns and a filtered set of rows. Also remember S Q L keywords like SELECT and FROM are case-insensitive, while table and column name sensitivity depends on the database. A foreign key error typically happens when you try to insert a child row referencing a parent id that doesn't exist; the fix is to insert the parent first or correct the referenced value. Duplicate key violations occur when you insert a row using a primary key already present; resolve this by using a new unique id or letting the database auto-generate the key if supported. Type mismatches appear when, for example, you compare strings to dates or insert a non-numeric value into an INTEGER column; ensure your client formats values according to the column types. Another subtle problem in sqlite3 is not turning on PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; without it, your schema's foreign key clauses exist but are not enforced during inserts. A troubleshooting workflow: read the error message carefully, identify the violated constraint, check the parent table for the referenced value, and re-run corrected statements. Concrete example: if inserting an event fails with a foreign key error for creator_id = 5, query Participants to see whether participant_id 5 exists, and if not, insert it first. Key takeaway: constraint errors are informative — use them as diagnostic signals to correct schema order or input values rather than seeing them as unexplained failures.

These three concept cards summarize the foundations you will rely on. First, the Relational Model: data is organized into tables of rows and columns, modeling entities in a predictable two-dimensional structure. Second, Table and Row: a table groups entries of the same entity type, and each row is a single record representing an instance of that entity. Third, Column and Data Type: columns are named attributes with types like INTEGER, VARCHAR, DATE, or TEXT that limit acceptable values and guide how comparisons behave. Keep these ideas in mind as you design schemas so that structure and data types match real-world attributes and queries behave as you expect. A quick mental check is to ask whether each table stores one entity type and whether each column has a clear type and purpose.

These three cards highlight keys and S Q L categories that structure how you build and operate on relational data. First, Primary Key: a unique, non-null column or columns that identify each row and support indexing and lookups. Second, Foreign Key: a column that references a primary key in another table to create relationships and enforce referential integrity. Third, S Q L categories — DDL and DML: DDL (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE) defines schema and constraints; DML (INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE) manipulates the data within those schemas. Remembering these distinctions helps you separate the act of defining structure from the act of changing data. A quick check: when you change a table's columns, you run DDL; when you add rows or query them, you use DML. Key takeaway: keys enforce identity and relationships, and S Q L provides distinct command families to define structure and to operate on rows.
